title: How to Text Your Crush: Openers, Topics and What Not to Send — cv.cm
description: How to text your crush without overthinking: good first messages, topics, how often to text, light flirting, when to stop, and how to move to a meeting.
h1: How do you text your crush without being awkward?
answer: Start with something specific to them, not just "hey". Ask real questions and answer theirs, match their energy and message length, and keep it light. Text when you have something to say, not on a schedule. If they reply with interest and ask things back, suggest a call or a meeting. If replies stay short for a week or two, slow down and let them come to you.

sections.h: The basic idea: a good chat is a two-way chat
body: Texting someone you like feels high-stakes, so people overthink every word. The good news is that the rules are simple and the same for anyone, whether you are writing to a girl, a guy, or anyone you like. A good chat goes both ways: each person shares something, asks something and answers what they were asked.

Research supports this. In studies by Karen Huang and colleagues at Harvard, people who asked more questions, especially follow-up questions about what the other person had just said, were liked more, including in speed dating, where they got more second dates. Follow-up questions show you were listening.

Another study, by Erica Boothby and colleagues, found that after a conversation people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them. They called this the liking gap. So if a chat felt a bit awkward to you, it probably felt better to them than you think.
The best opener connects to something real: a class you share, a post they made, something you talked about in person. It gives them an easy thing to reply to.

body: Do not wait for a perfect line. A simple, friendly, specific message is better than a clever one you sent too late.

sections.h: Topics that work and how to keep it going
body: Good topics are things the other person can talk about with pleasure. Start light and go deeper slowly as trust grows.

ul: Shared things: class, work, a friend group, a show you both watch.
Their interests: music, games, sports, cooking, travel. Ask what they like about it, not only what it is.
Small stories from the day: "The bus driver sang the whole way today."
Recommendations: food, songs, books. They are easy to answer and give you a reason to talk again.
Later, a little deeper: plans, what they are excited about, what their family is like.

body: To keep it going, use the simple pattern of answer, add, ask. If they ask "How was your weekend?", do not just say "Good". Try: "Good, I finally cleaned my room and then got hotpot with my cousin. How about you, did you go to the concert?"
Match their energy and length. If they send three lines, you can send three lines. If they send one, do not send ten paragraphs. If they use stickers or voice messages, you can too.

sections.h: How often to text, and how fast to reply
body: There is no correct number of messages a day. Early on, a few short exchanges a day, or a conversation every day or two, is common. Text when you have something to say. Reply when you see the message and have time. There is no need to wait a set number of minutes to look less interested; that kind of timing game mostly creates confusion.

A useful check is balance. Look at the last week. Do both of you start conversations? If you started almost every one, stop starting for a few days and see if they reach out. That is not a game; it is a fair way to see their interest.

body.note: Reply speed alone means little. People have work, school, family and different phone habits. Whether they ask you questions and keep the chat going matters much more.

sections.h: How to flirt lightly without being creepy
body: Light flirting is warm and playful, and it leaves the other person free to answer however they like. It is not pressure, and it is not about their body.

head: Send
Avoid
rows: "You have good taste in music. I'm stealing this playlist."
Comments about their body or what they are wearing
"Talking to you was the best part of my day."
"Why are you ignoring me?" after a short silence
"Okay, you win. Your hometown sounds better than mine."
Many messages in a row when they have not replied
"I'd like to hear that story in person sometime."
Sexual jokes or photos they did not ask for
A sticker or joke that fits something they said
Asking where they are and who they are with

body: If you are unsure whether a message is too much, ask yourself: would I be comfortable if they showed this to a friend? If not, do not send it. Sending sexual images to someone who did not clearly agree is never okay and is illegal in many places.

sections.h: Moving from texting to a call or a meeting
body: Texting is a way to get to know someone, not the goal. When the chat is warm for a week or two, suggest the next step.

ol: Suggest something linked to your chat: "You keep talking about that dumpling place. Want to go together on Friday?"
Make it specific and small: a day, a place, about an hour.
Give an easy way out: "No worries if you're busy."
If they say yes, confirm the day before with one short message.
If they say "maybe another time" without a new day, wait for them to suggest one.

body: If you are far apart, suggest a short video call instead: "Want to call for a bit tonight? Typing is too slow for this story." For more on invitations, see cv.cm's guide on how to ask someone out.

sections.h: When replies are short: what to do
body: Short replies can mean many things: they are busy, tired, shy over text, or not very interested. One short reply means little. A pattern over a week or two means more.

Suggest a call or meeting; some people are much warmer in person

Do not push; one friendly message, then wait
No reply to two messages in a row
Busy, lost interest, or avoiding

body: The kindest thing you can do for yourself is to stop chasing. You can send one easy last message, such as "No pressure at all, I just enjoyed talking. Have a good week." Then let it be. If you want a fuller read of what their messages may mean, see cv.cm's guide to signs someone likes you over text, or take the crush test.

ul: A long message confessing everything before you have spent much time together. Confess in person when the signs are good.
Guilt: "I guess I'm not important to you."
Tests: messages meant to see if they get jealous.
Screenshots of your chat sent to others to ask what it means. If they find out, it hurts trust.
Late-night messages after drinking that you would not send sober.
Anything after they clearly asked you to stop. Respect that right away.

faq.q: Should I text my crush first?
faq.a: Yes, if you want to talk to them. Who texts first does not decide interest; how the chat goes after that matters more.

faq.q: How do I start a conversation with a girl I like over text?
faq.a: The same way as with anyone: mention something specific you share or something she posted, and ask a question she can enjoy answering. Avoid comments about her looks as a first message.

faq.q: Is it bad to double text?
faq.a: One follow-up after a day or two is fine, especially if it adds something new. Many messages in a row with no reply puts pressure on the other person.

faq.q: How long should I wait to text back?
faq.a: Reply when you see it and have time. Waiting on purpose to look less interested usually creates confusion, not attraction.

faq.q: What do I do if my crush leaves me on read?
faq.a: Do nothing for a while. People read messages and forget to reply. If it keeps happening, take it as low interest and stop starting chats.
